meta.purpose: Real, sourced 2026 figures for charging an electric car at home and in public, for SLATE's money system.

conventions.confirmed: true means the figure was read on the cited page during this research (for PDFs, in the PDF text itself). false means it came only from a search-result summary or a page that could not be opened, and must be checked before use.
conventions.derived: Any 'derived' value was computed here by adding published components. It is arithmetic on sourced numbers, not a published figure, and says which components it adds.
conventions.currency: Each figure carries its own currency. US cents and dollars for the US places, CAD for Canada, MXN for Mexico, GBP pence for Great Britain, EUR cents for Ireland.
conventions.publicFastTrackerNote: US network averages come from DCFC Tracker, a third-party site that syncs the networks' public prices. Networks (Tesla, Electrify America, EVgo) publish prices only in their apps, not on a web price list, so no first-party per-state figure exists. DCFC Tracker records the peak rate where time-of-use pricing applies, and its averages are unweighted by site.

globalHomeShareFallback.value: EV owners charge privately (at home or a workplace) almost 75% of the time, and at public fast chargers only 10% of the time
globalHomeShareFallback.scope: worldwide survey data; no country breakdown for the US, Canada, UK, Ireland or Mexico
globalHomeShareFallback.publisher: International Energy Agency, Global EV Outlook 2026

registrations.definition: Records with record_type VEH and registration_class PAS (standard passenger plates) and a registration expiring on or after 2026-09-02. County is the owner's county of residence or use. Counting only PAS leaves out taxis, for-hire vehicles, vanity and special plate classes and commercial classes, so it undercounts cars on the road, most of all in NYC.
registrations.method: Counted by this research through the Socrata API (SoQL count over the dataset); not a figure DMV publishes as a total.
registrations.publisher: New York State DMV, on Open Data NY
registrations.note: The request asked for 2024 or 2025. The dataset is a rolling snapshot, not an annual series, so the count is as of September 2026.

shareDarkerThanLegal.finding: No published estimate was found, from any survey, agency or study, of the share of cars whose window tint is darker than the legal limit, in New York or anywhere in the US, Canada or the UK.
shareDarkerThanLegal.searched: NHTSA (its 1991 Report to Congress on window tinting and later interpretations cover what new cars transmit, not after-market compliance), NYS DMV, UK police and DVSA tint enforcement, and general survey searches. NY inspection has checked front-side tint since 2017, but DMV publishes no failure counts that were found.

relatedNyTicketCounts.note: Not a share of cars. Tickets for tint-type violations of VTL 375(12-a)(b) as recorded in DMV's ticket file. A ticket is not a vehicle, some drivers get several, and the windshield code also covers non-tint obstructions.
relatedNyTicketCounts.codesCounted: 37512A1 front windshield non-transparent, 37512A2 side wings / side windows non-transparent, 37512A3 rear side windows non-transparent
relatedNyTicketCounts.publisher: New York State DMV, 'Traffic Tickets Issued: Four Year Window', Open Data NY
relatedNyTicketCounts.coverageCaveat: The file draws on DMV's TSLED ticket records. Whether it fully covers tickets adjudicated by NYC's Traffic Violations Bureau was not confirmed, so NYC is likely undercounted.

uncertain: Con Ed TOU rates ($0.0522 off-peak, $0.2786 / $0.1711 peak): Con Ed says they exclude surcharges and taxes; whether they include supply was not confirmed.
Con Ed standard SC 1 monthly customer charge: not found. Only the TOU rate's $21.00 was read.
Eversource Rate 7 off-peak generation 10.629 cents (July to December 2026) and the exact 11.577-cent standard service figure: search summaries only.
LADWP 2026 tier totals: not published on the pages read. Only the 2025 totals and the 2026 adjustment factors were confirmed. The R-1B hours are from third-party summaries.
EIA California average (33.61 cents) is a poor proxy for LADWP, which is municipal and cheaper.
Ofgem London regional cap (26.60p, 42.92p/day): search summary only; Ofgem shows the GB average without a postcode.
Toronto all-in figures leave out the line-loss adjustment; Ontario Electricity Rebate and HST treatment follows Toronto Hydro's page but the combined arithmetic is this research's own.
Ontario public fast charging: no current first-party price for Petro-Canada, FLO, Ivy or Tesla Canada. Ivy's $0.62/kWh dates from November 2023.
BC Hydro: effective dates were not on the pages; search summaries give slightly different April 2026 figures (11.72 / 23.30). Tax treatment and a reported move to a blended flat rate are unconfirmed.

Mexico: CFE's own pages could not be read (bot wall, TLS error). Tarifa 1 prices come from a secondary page citing CFE; block limits, DAC's Central-region price and all Tesla Mexico prices are unconfirmed. No CFE residential TOU or EV tariff was found.
Ireland: prices are Electric Ireland's, one supplier among several, not a regulated national price. ESB ecars may raise prices again in October 2026.

Home share: no measured, country-specific share of charging energy done at home was found for any of the eight places. The US figure is an NREL 2030 projection; the Canada figure is a share of owners, not energy; the UK figure is access, not energy; the IEA global 75% (private, including workplace) is the only energy-use figure.
US public fast-charging averages come from a third-party tracker (DCFC Tracker), record peak prices, and are state-level, not city-level.
Tint: NY passenger count uses only the PAS registration class and is a September 2026 snapshot, not 2024 or 2025. No estimate of the share of cars with illegal tint exists that was found.
